planting.note: Set rooted cuttings into a sharply drained scree, trough, or tufa crevice mix with the woody crown held just above grade so winter moisture never collects around it.

directions: This cushion-forming alpine shrub clings naturally to limestone cliff faces in the Italian and Austrian Alps, so garden success depends on mimicking that vertical, gritty, fast-draining habitat rather than planting it in ordinary border soil. Tuck plants into a tufa rock crevice, raised scree bed, or alpine trough using a mix heavy in grit and lean in organic matter, and keep the crown dry through winter since standing moisture around the woody base is the most common cause of failure. In late spring it covers itself in intensely fragrant, deep rose-pink flowers held tight against the foliage, with the selection 'Grandiflora' offering notably larger blooms than the wild type. Growth is extremely slow and plants resent root disturbance, so start from a small rooted cutting and leave it undisturbed for years rather than attempting to divide or transplant an established specimen.

planting.note: Plant small rooted cuttings in a gritty, neutral-to-alkaline scree or trough mix with sharp drainage, giving light shade from the hottest afternoon sun in warmer climates.

directions: Native to rocky limestone outcrops in Greece and the Balkans, this dwarf shrub forms a tight, woody cushion only a couple of inches tall that spreads slowly outward across scree or trough surfaces. Clusters of small white flowers flushed pink on the reverse open in late spring and carry a sweet jasmine-like fragrance well out of proportion to their size. It wants sharp drainage and a lean, gritty substrate above all else, and in hot summer climates benefits from a touch of afternoon shade or a position where surrounding rocks shield the roots from excessive heat. Because it is slow to establish and dislikes disturbance, it is best purchased or propagated as a small cutting-grown plant and left to mature in place in a trough or raised rock garden rather than moved once settled.

planting.note: Sow directly onto gritty, well-drained soil in a sunny rock garden position, since this short-lived mountain species self-sows readily where happy and is often treated as a biennial.

directions: This subalpine European native forms a low rosette of soft, hairy leaves in its first season before sending up slender stems of nodding, one-sided clusters of pale to deep blue bells the following year, each flower fringed on the inside with the fine hairs that give the species its common name. It is a true mountain meadow plant, wanting cool summers, sharp drainage, and full sun, and it often behaves as a short-lived perennial or biennial, declining after flowering but readily reseeding itself in gritty rock garden soil. Unlike many of its clump-forming relatives already common in cultivation, it is grown almost exclusively from seed and resents being coddled with rich, moisture-retentive soil. Deadheading spent spikes encourages a longer self-sown presence in the garden over successive years.

planting.note: Sow or plant into a vertical tufa crevice or deep scree with sharp winter drainage, since this limestone specialist resents standing moisture around its crown far more than cold.

directions: Found wild only in limestone crevices of the Julian and southeastern Alps, this is among the most sought-after plants in alpine and rock garden societies for its uniquely shaped flower: a pale lavender-blue tube that pinches sharply inward at the mouth, unlike the open bells of nearly every other campanula. It forms a tight tuft of small rounded leaves wedged into narrow rock fissures, so in cultivation it is best grown vertically in a tufa block or deep crevice bed rather than flat ground, which keeps its crown shielded from pooling winter wet. Flowering comes in mid to late summer on wiry stems barely a few inches tall. Because it is slow-growing and particular about drainage, gardeners typically start it from fresh seed or small nursery divisions rather than attempting cuttings.

planting.note: Plant young container-grown trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun, since established Judas trees resist transplanting and are best sited once as a small specimen.

directions: A small deciduous tree native across the Mediterranean basin and into western Asia, this species produces its vivid magenta-pink, pea-family flowers directly on bare trunks and older branches in early spring, well before the heart-shaped blue-green leaves unfurl, giving the whole tree a startling clothed-in-blossom appearance. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, and lean alkaline soils far better than most flowering ornamentals, and it is a long-lived, trouble-free choice for a sunny courtyard or Mediterranean-style planting. It is usually raised from seed, which benefits from scarification and a period of cold stratification to break dormancy, and young trees should be planted into their permanent position while still small, since the taproot makes later transplanting difficult. Flat seedpods that persist into winter are an attractive secondary feature and give the tree one of its common names.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, giving it room to develop into a large upright specimen.

directions: Collected from the mountains of Yunnan by the French missionary-botanist for whom it is named, this vigorous Chinese mock orange is distinguished from the many European and hybrid Philadelphus already in cultivation by its striking purple-tinged calyces, which form a dark contrasting cup behind each pure white, intensely fragrant flower in early summer. It grows into a large, upright, somewhat open shrub well suited to the back of a mixed border or a naturalistic woodland-edge planting where its size and informal habit have room to develop. Culture is the same as other mock oranges: plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, and renew the shrub's vigor every few years by removing a portion of the oldest flowering canes right after bloom finishes. It is propagated from softwood cuttings taken in early summer rather than from seed, which is rarely produced or offered commercially.
